w: What's tested The female reproductive organs and their jobs, and the ovary's two functions: gametes and steroids Oogenesis: the oocyte numbers and the two meiotic arrests, prophase I and metaphase II The five follicle stages, how to identify each one under the microscope, and the layers of the Graafian follicle's wall What FSH and LH each do: FSH grows the follicles, the LH surge matures and ovulates the dominant one Ovulation: the LH surge, rupture of the follicle, the corpus luteum and the corpus albicans How the ovarian and uterine cycles line up, day by day, and his cycle graph of FSH, LH, estrogen and progesterone Stratum functionalis versus stratum basalis, their two kinds of artery, and what starts menstruation The wall and lining of the uterine tube, uterus, cervix and vagina The mammary gland, and milk production (prolactin) versus milk ejection (oxytocin) Dr. Herr gives this histology lecture, the companion to his male reproductive histology lecture. These notes follow his recording, which he made and posted on the afternoon of Friday, November 6, and his slides. At the end he says that if you came to class that day, you already know what to focus on; the points he stresses in the recording are marked here, and where his slides mark a point with asterisks, the notes say so. The organs and what they do The internal organs are the ovaries, the oviducts, the uterus, the cervix and the vagina. The external genitalia are the labial folds, the clitoris and the vestibule, which he says he will not discuss. The mammary glands are not really part of the reproductive system, but they are accessory organs related to it developmentally and functionally, so they close the lecture. Ovaries Serve both endocrine and exocrine functions: they produce gametes and steroid hormones Oviducts (uterine or fallopian tubes) Conduct ova to the uterus Uterus Receives the zygote for implantation at the blastula stage, conducts sperm up to the oviducts, and is the muscular sac where the fetus develops and from which it is expelled Cervix The opening of the uterus into the vagina Vagina The canal that receives the sperm Fertilization happens in the uterine tube, so sperm have to get all the way there; the tube's fimbriae catch the oocyte like a catcher's mitt. He skips the 3D anatomy of the broad ligament. These organs go through regular cyclic changes from puberty to menopause, driven by neural activity and hormones during each menstrual cycle and during pregnancy. Menarche, the start of menstrual cycles, usually comes between 9 and 14 years of age. Menopause, when the ovaries stop both their reproductive and their endocrine functions, usually comes between 45 and 55. His slide gives a cycle of 28 to 30 days; later in the recording he says 28 to 33 several times. Normal cycles vary. The ovary: two functions, two regions The paired ovaries sit in the pelvis. Each is almond shaped, about 3 by 1.5 by 2 centimeters. They have two primary functions. The first is making gametes, called oogenesis: developing gametes are oocytes, and mature gametes are ova. The second is making steroids. Estrogens promote the growth and maturation of the internal and external sex organs. Progestogens prepare the internal sex organs for pregnancy by promoting secretory changes in the endometrium. Keep that split in mind: it explains the two halves of the uterine cycle later. A section of the ovary shows a central medulla and a peripheral cortex. The medulla is loose connective tissue rich in blood vessels and nerves. The cortex holds the developing ovarian follicles. Drawings show the stages in a circle, but follicles develop all over the cortex. Over the surface is an epithelium continuous with the mesothelium. It is often called the germinal epithelium, but the name is a holdover: it does not house germ cells and does not give rise to gametes. The ovary's capsule is the tunica albuginea, which the mature follicle has to break through at ovulation. Oogenesis: the numbers Primordial germ cells enter the gonad and become oogonia, which stay diploid and divide by mitosis. That mitotic activity continues until about the 5th fetal month, when there are about 5 to 7 million primary oocytes. Only about 1 to 2 million become surrounded by follicular cells and survive to birth; the rest degenerate and die. The survivors are primary oocytes arrested in prophase of meiosis I. The losses continue through childhood: of about a million that become primordial follicles, about 600,000 become atretic, so at menarche only about 400,000 remain. From then on, ovulation generally happens every 28 days for the next 30 to 40 years, one oocyte a month, for a total of only about 450 oocytes released over the reproductive years. Each month about 12 follicles begin to develop, but typically only one dominant follicle ovulates a secondary oocyte. The rest become atretic: they die by apoptosis. 5th fetal month About 5 to 7 million primary oocytes; oogonia stop dividing Birth About 1 to 2 million, each in a follicle, arrested in prophase I Menarche About 400,000 Each month About 12 follicles start to grow; usually one ovulates Whole reproductive span About 450 ovulated The two meiotic arrests The oocyte stops twice on its way through meiosis, and each stop is released by a different event. Marked with three asterisks on his slide, and said in the recording: all follicles within the ovary contain a primary oocyte arrested in prophase I. The LH surge causes the primary oocyte to complete meiosis I shortly before ovulation, producing a secondary oocyte. The secondary oocyte enters meiosis II and arrests at metaphase II until fertilization. Arrest one, prophase of meiosis I. Set up before birth and held for years, in every follicle, at every stage up to the dominant Graafian follicle. Granulosa cells of antral follicles secrete oocyte maturation inhibitor, or OMI, into the antrum, which fits with the oocyte staying put. Release one: the LH surge. It causes release of a meiosis-inducing factor, and the primary oocyte completes meiosis I just before ovulation. Arrest two, metaphase of meiosis II. The new secondary oocyte goes straight into meiosis II, lines its chromosomes up on the metaphase plate and stops. This is the cell that is ovulated. (Reading one slide aloud he says "enters prophase"; the slide and his earlier summary say metaphase II.) Release two: fertilization. Only upon fertilization does the oocyte complete the second meiotic division, forming the ovum and a second polar body. Unfertilized, it stays viable about 24 hours. The first meiotic division ends with unequal cytokinesis: the cytoplasm is split so that one daughter cell keeps most of it and the other, the polar body, gets only a small ring. So meiosis I gives one large secondary oocyte and the first polar body, and the egg keeps its large store of cytoplasm. Compare spermatogenesis in the male lecture: it has no long arrests, and each primary spermatocyte gives four spermatids, where each primary oocyte gives one egg. Follicle stage one: the primordial follicle An ovarian follicle is an oocyte surrounded by one or more layers of epithelial cells. It passes through five basic stages: primordial, early primary (unilaminar), late primary (multilaminar), secondary (antral), and the mature Graafian follicle. The primordial follicle is the most primitive. It is a primary oocyte, arrested in prophase I, surrounded by a single layer of squamous follicular cells on a basal lamina. These flat cells completely surround the oocyte and are attached to each other by desmosomes. The oocyte is a very small spherical cell, about 25 micrometers across on his slide, with an asymmetric nucleus, vesicular-looking chromatin and prominent organelles. Stage two: the early primary (unilaminar) follicle Primary follicles develop from primordial follicles. The change you can see is that the follicular cells become cuboidal; from this stage on they are called granulosa cells. While there is still a single layer, the follicle is unilaminar. The oocyte grows into a very large cell, about four times its starting size (100 to 150 micrometers on the slide), with a large nucleus and abundant rough ER, Golgi and mitochondria. The zona pellucida begins to form, rich in glycosaminoglycans and glycoproteins. The granulosa cells develop extensive gap junctions with each other but no tight junctions, so there is no blood-follicle barrier. Compare the testis, where tight junctions between Sertoli cells form the blood-testis barrier. Stage three: the late primary (multilaminar) follicle Granulosa cells proliferate into several layers, so the follicle is now multilaminar, and cortical granules start to develop at the outer edge of the oocyte. The zona pellucida surrounds the oocyte; it is produced by the follicular cells, and it is made of glycoproteins. His slide names them ZP1, ZP2 and ZP3, and he says you don't need to know those. Microvilli from the oocyte and filopodia from the granulosa cells penetrate the zona and touch each other, so the cells stay in contact across it. Outside the basal lamina of the granulosa cells, stromal cells organize into the theca folliculi, which has two layers: Theca interna: richly vascularized connective tissue. Its cells have LH receptors, and in response to LH they make androgens that are precursors to estrogen. Theca externa: mostly fibrous connective tissue and smooth muscle cells. Stage four: the secondary (antral) follicle A secondary follicle is distinguished from a primary follicle by one thing: liquor folliculi, the follicle's fluid. Under the influence of FSH, granulosa cells produce it, and it contains glycosaminoglycans, proteoglycans and steroid-binding proteins, along with steroids such as progesterone and estradiol. Granulosa cells also secrete oocyte maturation inhibitor into it. It first collects in small pools within the granulosa layer (Call-Exner bodies), which merge into a single chamber, the antrum. A cumulus oophorus forms: a mound of granulosa cells that holds the oocyte. The single layer of granulosa cells wrapped around the primary oocyte is the corona radiata. Cortical granules are now evident just under the oocyte's plasma membrane. The oocyte is still a primary oocyte in prophase I. Stage five: the mature Graafian follicle The Graafian follicle, named for Reinier de Graaf, is the follicle that undergoes ovulation and releases the secondary oocyte. It is quite large, about 20 millimeters, and makes a bulge on the surface of the ovary. Its antrum is much bigger, its theca layers are more prominent, and the oocyte adheres to the wall of the follicle through the cumulus oophorus. His slide marks the time scale, and he stresses it: growth from a primordial to a mature follicle takes many months, not one 28- to 33-day cycle. On a section of the Graafian follicle's wall he names the layers from the antrum outward, and says you can tell them apart on a histological slide: the granulosa layer, a very thin basement membrane, the theca interna, and the theca externa. FSH and LH split the work, and he went back a few slides to show it again: an FSH surge induces the growth of 10 to 12 antral follicles, one of which becomes dominant, with a huge antrum; it takes LH, in the FSH plus LH surge, to trigger maturation and ovulation of that dominant follicle. Dr. Madison covers the hypothalamic-pituitary axis behind it. Telling the stages apart Under the microscope, ask four questions in order. Are the follicular cells flat or cuboidal? Is there one layer or several? Is there fluid? Is the follicle big enough to bulge from the ovary? Primordial One layer, squamous, joined by desmosomes Oocyte about 25 micrometers; no zona pellucida Early primary (unilaminar) One layer, cuboidal granulosa cells Zona pellucida starting to form; gap junctions Late primary (multilaminar) Several layers of granulosa cells Full zona; theca interna and externa organizing Secondary (antral) Many layers, with fluid among them Liquor folliculi and antrum; cumulus oophorus; corona radiata Graafian Granulosa cells around a large antrum About 20 millimeters; bulges on the ovary; prominent theca Ovulation: the endocrine events The dominant follicle sets off its own ovulation. Estrogen released from the Graafian follicle raises the blood estrogen level, and that increases LH production: the LH surge. On his graph the estrogen peak comes just before the LH peak. Here a rising hormone drives the pituitary signal up rather than down: the positive feedback that L16 covers. The LH surge does two things at the follicle: It increases blood flow to the follicle and the permeability of the capillaries in the theca interna, which leads to local edema, or swelling. (He reads this as the theca externa in the recording; his slide says theca interna, the vascular layer.) It causes the release of meiosis-inducing factor, which signals the primary oocyte to complete meiosis I, giving a secondary oocyte and one polar body. The secondary oocyte immediately enters meiosis II and stops at metaphase. Ovulation: what happens in the ovary Granulosa cells of the Graafian follicle keep producing glycosaminoglycans and hyaluronic acid, which hold fluid, mostly water, so the antrum swells. The follicle enlarges, moves to the outer cortex and pushes against the capsule, the tunica albuginea, until the walls of both the ovary and the follicle rupture. The secondary oocyte and the cells of the corona radiata are released into the peritoneum, the abdominal cavity, near the opening of the oviduct, the infundibulum, which has to catch them and send them into the tube. The emptied follicle collapses and becomes folded, and LH converts it into the corpus luteum. After ovulation: corpus luteum and corpus albicans Granulosa-lutein cells come from the granulosa cells of the Graafian follicle and make progesterone and estrogen. Theca-lutein cells come from the enlarged cells of the theca interna and make progesterone. Together they make up the corpus luteum; its hormones make the progesterone peak on his graph. If pregnancy does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates, and the old structure fills with fibroblasts that secrete collagen, becoming the white corpus albicans. If pregnancy does occur, the placenta produces a hormone that helps maintain the corpus luteum, and with it the progesterone that keeps the endometrium in place. How the ovarian and uterine cycles line up The ovary and the uterus run one 28-day cycle together, and two of the uterine phases even carry the ovarian names. 1 to 5 Menstrual Corpus luteum gone; new follicles starting Functionalis shed; basalis stays 5 to 14 Proliferative, or follicular Follicles grow and make estrogen; ovulation at the end Basalis rebuilds the functionalis 15 to 28 Secretory, or luteal Corpus luteum makes progesterone Thick functionalis; glands secrete The logic follows from the two steroids. Estrogen from the growing follicles drives growth, so the endometrium proliferates. Progesterone from the corpus luteum drives the secretory changes that prepare it for a pregnancy. One of his slides follows the uterine glands through the cycle: their cells and glandular tissue change a great deal. In standard histology they are straight and narrow while the functionalis regrows, then coiled and full of secretion in the secretory phase. When the corpus luteum fails, progesterone drops and the functionalis is lost. He walks through his cycle graph, days 1 to 28, line by line: Ovary: primary, secondary and vesicular follicles grow over days 1 to about 9 or 10; ovulation comes between days 13 and 15; then the corpus luteum, its regression, and the corpus albicans. FSH: higher for the first 7 to 9 days, a small dip, then a peak right before ovulation together with LH; low after ovulation, rising again at the end of the cycle. LH: baseline, then the big peak with FSH just before ovulation; it falls back and returns a little later. Estrogen: low, rising from about day 7 to a peak around day 12 or 13, a dip around days 15 to 17, a second, smaller rise around days 23 to 24, then down. Progesterone: low until about day 14, then rising gradually to a peak around day 22, and back down by about day 28. His graph and his words give FSH a peak with LH at ovulation, a smaller peak than LH's, and the hub follows him in every lecture, the cycle figure included. L16's slide puts it differently (inhibin holding FSH down at midcycle); most physiology texts draw the small FSH peak beside the LH surge, as he does. The uterine tube The oviduct is the conduit for sperm to reach the secondary oocyte and for the fertilized ovum to reach the uterus. It has four regions, from the ovary inward: Infundibulum: the funnel-shaped segment, covered by fimbriae, that receives the ovulated oocyte. Ampulla: the broadest, swollen segment, usually the site of fertilization. Isthmus: the narrow region between the ampulla and the uterus. Intramural region: where the tube passes into the uterine wall. "I do want you to know some components of this," he says of the tube's cells and layers. Its mucosa has longitudinal folds in all regions. The epithelium is simple columnar with two cell types: ciliated cells, whose wave of cilia is directed toward the uterus, and non-ciliated peg cells, which secrete a fluid that provides nutrients to the ovum. The muscularis is a poorly defined inner circular and outer longitudinal layer of smooth muscle, not built for strong peristalsis, and the outer serosa is a simple squamous membrane. His slide flags two points about the tube. First, the mucosa provides nutrients and protection for the oocyte and the sperm, and it produces factors that promote sperm activation, a process called capacitation. In the male lecture the epididymis holds capacitation back, so it happens only in the female tract. Second, the oocyte remains viable for only about 24 hours if it is not fertilized. The uterus and its three layers The uterus is a single, thick, pear-shaped, active muscular organ, about 7 by 5 by 2.5 centimeters and 30 to 40 grams, with the oviducts entering near its broad end. It has three regions: the body, the central, broad portion the oviducts enter; the fundus, the rounded topmost region above the openings of the oviducts; and the cervix, the neck, a narrow, circular portion that protrudes and opens into the vagina. Its wall has three layers, from the inside out: Endometrium: the mucosa, next to the lumen, split into the stratum functionalis and the stratum basalis. Myometrium: most of the uterus. Inner longitudinal, middle circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle. The middle circular layer carries numerous large blood vessels and is called the stratum vasculare. Perimetrium: a very thin outer serous layer, the visceral peritoneal covering. The endometrium: functionalis and basalis The endometrium is simple columnar epithelium, with both ciliated and nonciliated cells, over a lamina propria full of simple branched glands that extend down toward the myometrium. It has two layers that behave very differently, and the reason is their blood supply. The uterine artery sends up two kinds of branch: spiral arteries to the functionalis and straight (basal) arteries to the basalis. Where Superficial, toward the lumen Deep and narrow, next to the myometrium Blood supply Many helical, or spiral, arteries Its own straight (basal) arteries, so it is spared when the spiral arteries constrict In the cycle Undergoes extreme changes; shed at menstruation Changes little; its glands and connective tissue proliferate to rebuild the functionalis Menstruation Marked with three asterisks on his slide, and explained twice in the recording: the drop in progesterone causes constriction of the spiral arteries, leading to local ischemia in the functional layer and its separation from the basal layer. Follow the chain. No pregnancy, so the corpus luteum degenerates. Progesterone falls. The spiral arteries of the functionalis contract periodically and cut off its oxygen, so the functionalis becomes hypoxic. The hypoxia breaks down the spiral arteries, which flood the lamina propria with blood, and the functionalis, its glands and decidua-like cells, detaches and is shed into the uterine cavity: menses, days 1 to 5. The basalis is not really affected, because its straight arteries give it an independent blood supply, and it regrows a new functionalis in the proliferative phase. The myometrium The size and number of myometrial muscle cells are related to the estrogen level. During pregnancy the muscle cells show both hypertrophy, an increase in cell size, and hyperplasia, an increase in the number of smooth muscle cells. He left this slide for you to read. The cervix Cervix means neck. The cervix is the terminal end of the uterus, protruding into the vagina, with an internal and an external os. Its canal is lined by mucus-secreting simple columnar cells that form glandular crypts. Its secretions change with the reproductive state: At ovulation, the cervical glands secrete a watery fluid that helps sperm migrate (on his slide). During pregnancy, the secretions are more viscous and form a plug that keeps microorganisms and sperm out of the uterus: the cervix essentially closes off. The part of the cervix that projects into the vagina is covered with stratified squamous epithelium. The abrupt change between the two linings is the transformation zone. The vagina The vaginal wall is devoid of glands. Cells of its mucosa produce local secretions, as do the vestibular glands enclosed within the labia, and the mucus associated with ovulation comes from the glands of the cervix. The tissue is rich in elastic fibers and leukocytes and has few sensory nerves; most sensation comes from the external genitalia. The vaginal epithelium also undergoes cyclic changes during the menstrual cycle. The wall has three layers: Mucosa: stratified squamous epithelium over a highly vascular lamina propria with high numbers of lymphocytes and neutrophils. Muscular layer: mainly longitudinal bundles of smooth muscle. Adventitia: dense connective tissue. The epithelial cells synthesize and store glycogen, which is released as they desquamate. The natural bacteria there are mostly Lactobacillus species, which break the glycogen down to lactic acid. The lactic acid keeps the vaginal surface acidic, which inhibits the growth of pathogens. So anything that wipes out the lactobacilli, such as a course of antibiotics, takes away that acid defense. The linings side by side Uterine tube Simple columnar Ciliated cells plus peg cells; longitudinal folds Endometrium Simple columnar Simple branched glands in the lamina propria Cervical canal Simple columnar, mucus-secreting Glandular crypts; watery or viscous mucus Vagina, and the cervix where it projects into it Stratified squamous Glycogen-rich cells; no glands in the vaginal wall The mammary gland The mammary gland is made of tubuloalveolar glands in 15 to 20 lobes radiating out from the nipple, separated from each other by adipose and collagenous connective tissue; several ducts open at one nipple, through the lactiferous sinuses. A resting, nonsecreting gland is built like a lactating one but is much smaller. During lactation the terminal portions of the ducts branch and grow and develop secretory alveolar units. His slide, which he reads aloud, ties the start of lactation to surges of estrogen and progesterone during pregnancy and after giving birth. His slides show the gland at puberty and in pregnancy, as it grows toward that lactating form. Milk: production versus ejection Human milk contains carbohydrate (lactose), proteins (caseins), lipids, IgA, minerals and electrolytes, and it is rich in antibodies. Two hormones split the work: Synthesis, or production Prolactin Secretion, or ejection (let-down) Oxytocin Colostrum is the milk produced for the first 3 to 4 days after birth. It has increased concentrations of proteins and immunoglobulin A, so a new mother's first milk is the most antibody-rich, not the weakest.
